results.summary: This design implements several free-running oscillators built from combinational loops with dividers to bring the output frequency below 50 kHz, plus a true random number generator output. The user selects one of three oscillator sources via input pins and can observe the generated clock, divided versions, and the TRNG bit on the outputs. Testing requires measuring the output frequency with external equipment and observing the random bit stream. The project is intended to compare simulation against silicon reality and is documented only briefly.

This Verilog design generates a PWM signal whose duty cycle is selected by three digital input signals, stepping in 12.5% increments from 12.5% to 100% when enabled. It is tested by applying logic combinations to the speed inputs with enable high and viewing the resulting pulse width on an oscilloscope. External hardware needed includes a signal generator for the 10 MHz clock and an oscilloscope to observe the output. The documentation is in Spanish and describes a straightforward educational PWM exercise.

This Wokwi project uses OR gate logic to drive a seven-segment LED display so that it spells the letter J. The user flips input switches to generate the letter J on the display. The documentation does not specify which external hardware, if any, is required beyond the display itself. The project is very thin on technical detail and appears to be a simple educational or template exercise.

This design implements Wolfram's Rule 30 one-dimensional cellular automaton in hardware, storing a 320-bit generation that updates in parallel and is rendered as a 640x480 VGA image. Each frame starts from a single seed cell and displays 480 generations of chaotic evolution, with four selectable color palettes controlled by two input pins. It is tested by connecting a VGA monitor through the Tiny VGA Pmod, setting a 25 MHz clock, and releasing reset to see the triangular chaos pattern. The project is notable for directly implementing a chaotic automaton that was historically used as a random number generator.

This analog project is a double inverter buffer made of one large and one small inverter connected in series, originating from Matt's analog course. The analog input is on ua[1] and the buffered output is on ua[0], with no external hardware required. It is tested simply by applying an analog signal to the input and observing the output. The documentation is minimal and the design serves as an educational analog test structure.

This Wokwi puzzle game challenges the player to make a seven-segment display show all numbers from 0 to 9 by flipping switches, where each switch toggles a segment and its neighbors. It is tested by connecting microswitches to inputs i0 through i6 and a seven-segment display to outputs o0 through o6, with the decimal point unused. External hardware required includes a seven-segment LED display and seven microswitches. The project is a simple interactive logic puzzle with clear documentation.

This Verilog design generates a controllable Archimedean spiral pattern (r=theta) rendered on a VGA display. It is tested by setting the clock to 25 MHz and connecting a VGA Pmod, with input values altering the foreground/background colors and the speed of the spiral. External hardware needed includes a VGA Pmod and optionally switches for control. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the visual output and basic operation.

This Verilog design classifies images of numbers from 0 to 7 using the 16 most significant pixels of an 8x8 image as input features, and displays the result on a seven-segment display. It is tested by manually setting the feature inputs to match the pixel pattern of a digit, with an example provided for the digit zero. No external hardware is required. The project is a small educational machine-learning inference example with clear documentation of the feature mapping.

This design is a 4-neuron spiking neural network accelerator using the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire model, with weights held off-chip by an RP2040 and streamed in via PIO to keep the transistor budget under 2000. It processes one neuron at a time through a 7-state FSM, achieving about 1.78 million network passes per second at 50 MHz, and supports Hebbian LTP learning signaled through an output pulse. Testing requires an RP2040 running weight-streaming firmware, though a minimal smoke test can be done by injecting external spikes and observing spike outputs and FSM state pins. The project is notable for its time-multiplexed architecture and detailed interface documentation.

This Verilog project is a loopback tile with input skew measurement that counts up to 10, one second at a time, and displays the count on a seven-segment display. The documentation states that the how-it-works and how-to-test sections still need to be written, so the exact operation is unclear. External hardware mentioned includes programmable delay lines on the inputs. Because the documentation is essentially incomplete, the design's behavior and testing procedure cannot be fully described.
